headline: Post-Blow Edge Turns On Yellowfin at Wilmington — Widest Break of the Season
subhead: A stiff northeast blow left behind the sharpest temperature wall we've seen all year, and the tuna found it fast.
body_markdown:
Last week's blow did us a favor, even if it didn't feel that way while we were riding it out at the dock. Three days of northeast wind stacked cool shelf water up against the Gulf Stream filament pushing off Wilmington, and when it finally laid down Tuesday night the break that set up was the real deal — better than a ten degree spread from the 100-fathom line out to the canyon wall, which is about as wide as I've seen this edge get in July. That kind of contrast doesn't happen by accident. The upwelling stacked cold, bait-rich shelf water against the warm plume, and everything that swims got pinned right on that seam. New moon coming through mid-week is darkening the nights fast, which matters more than people think — squid don't show under a bright moon the same way, and with this being the first real dark stretch since the solstice, the underwater light guys are going to have their best shot of the month working the midshore breaks after dark.

Looking at the week ahead, Wednesday and Thursday are the window I'd circle. The edge won't hold this sharp forever — these filaments slide, and this one likely drifts east or gets chewed up by the next frontal push by the weekend. Winds look manageable through Thursday, building again Friday into the new-moon spring tide setup that's going to matter more for the guys working bays and inlets than for us offshore. For canyon work, the play this week is get out early in the window before it closes.

We ran the seam Tuesday between Wilmington and Poor Man's, working the color change where it was running about ten degrees warmer on the east side versus the shelf water to the west. Marked bait stacked heavy right on that line and it didn't take long — yellowfin from 35 to 55 pounds came up on a spread of medium-rigged ballyhoo behind Islander bars, green-and-black and blue-white running the long riggers, naked ballyhoo skipping the shorts. Trolled 6 to 7 knots right along the temp break, not over it — the fish were sitting on the warm side and ambushing anything that crossed. We had a double-digit day, not a fifty-fish day, but for the first real window since the last blow, I'll take it. A few of the boats working the Hudson east wall reported similar action, same warm seam pushing that far north, so if Wilmington's crowded or blown out, that's your backup.

Bigeye showed too, but only on the drop-back after dark — one boat chunking butterfish over the top of the canyon in 750 fathoms picked up a pair around midnight, working the current edge where the water goes from green to that deep cobalt blue. If you're going to chunk instead of troll, that's the play right now — wait for last light, set up on the upcurrent side of the break, and let the scent trail work while the sun goes down. Wahoo have been mixed in as a bycatch on the high-speed lures worked wide of the spread — nothing consistent enough to target specifically yet, but a couple fish in the 40-pound class came over the rail on blue-white Ilanders run off the shotgun. Mahi have been scattered around any floating debris or weed lines crossing the seam — small stuff mostly, schoolies in the 5 to 10 pound range, but worth a stop if you see color change or a mat of Sargassum.

The other story this week is midshore, and it's a different animal entirely. The northeast wind that built our canyon break also sharpened up the 20 to 30 fathom structure closer to the beach, and the Coimbra wreck corridor has bluefin stacking on it at around 20 fathoms. These aren't giants — schoolies and mediums mixing in — but they're eating well on the overnight squid bite. Underwater lights, small strips of squid or sabiki-jigged live squid on light circle hooks, fished right on bottom structure after dark. With the moon going dark through the weekend, this is the best window we'll get all month for that program. It's a shorter run than the canyon trip and a good option if the offshore forecast doesn't cooperate.

White marlin watch is still just that — a watch. No flags reported out of Wilmington yet, but the warm plume pushing toward the bank is exactly the trigger we look for, and historically it's about a week to ten days from first sighting to first real bite once that water gets established. I'd keep a pitch bait rigged on the flat lines starting now, just in case one shows early behind the dredge.

If I had one day this week, I'd take Wednesday, run straight to the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam at first light, and troll the break hard for four hours before it either produces or doesn't. Plan B is dropping south toward the canyon head to chunk after dark if the troll bite dies with the sun. Either way, this is the best structural setup we've had all season — whether it holds through the weekend is the only question left.
